extracted.intended_audience: editors, essayists, and contributors/readers of The Spectator; literary critics and textual editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for editing, composing, and judging prose and verse in the Spectator/familiar-essay tradition: (a) textual-criticism rules for presenting variant readings of poems and (b) rhetorical/style advice for essays, dedications, and social satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collate and print 'Various Readings' from editions and manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting an older poem in a new edition, give the several various readings which are found in former editions and in ancient manuscripts; present those variant readings to the public rather than silently adopting a single form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply the different readings stanza-by-stanza/verse-by-verse; explain variant forms and which authorities (Aldus, Vatican Manuscript, Cotton Library, German manuscript, etc.) support them; include footnotes with commentary. Example language on the page: 'I present to the Publick in a new Edition, with the several various Readings which I find of it in former Editions, and in Ancient Manuscripts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readings that preserve metre and rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: Restore genuine readings when variants would 'hurt the Metre' or break established rhyme; metrical integrity is a primary criterion in choosing among manuscript variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply prosodic devices (e.g., synæresis) when appropriate to save the metre; reject an editor's reading if it would make the line metrically faulty. Example: choosing 'e'er' over 'ever' because 'ever would' would 'hurt the Metre' and restoring 'Nor e'er would settle in my Heart.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh sense and etymology as grounds for emendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the semantic fit and etymology of a word before changing a reading; if an alternative reading better explains the author's intention or gives an intelligible derivation, that is a reason to alter the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linguistic/etymological reasoning (e.g., deriving 'Pelvidera' from pelvis meaning looking-glass) to propose emendations, but balance against manuscript authority. The editor notes the temptation to change 'Belvidera' to 'Pelvidera' because of etymology but resists if manuscripts disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for common transcriber errors (punctuation, cyphers, mistaken letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize predictable copying mistakes—misreading ampersand vs 'and', dash mistaken for stroke/letter, omission of cypher in numerals, confusion between similar letters—and use that knowledge when deciding readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples and reasoning in notes: ampersand (&) read as separate letters; a dash after '1' misread as a second figure leading '1'+'-' -> '2'; 'I' mistaken for 'T' because of dash; recommend skepticism about variants that look like the result of a transcription habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer judgment when manuscript evidence is inconclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: If many ancient manuscripts differ and there is significant uncertainty, leave the matter undecided rather than forcing an emendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state uncertainty and avoid dogmatic corrections: 'But this I shall leave to the Learned, without determining any thing in a Matter of so great Uncertainty.' Use explanatory notes rather than unilateral textual change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose persuasive moral essays by weaving classical, fable, and scriptural exempla
rubrics_metrics.description: Support a moral thesis (e.g., the virtue of Hope) by citing ancient poets, fables (Pandora's box), and scripture (the Psalmist), and by drawing reflective moral conclusions for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixture of authority (classical and biblical quotations), illustrative fable or anecdote, and a clear practical moral. The essay on Hope models: state thesis, give classical and fable evidence, draw two concise reflections, then close with a scriptural passage to reinforce the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual/sensory imagery (sight) as primary means to engage and transport readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on 'the Sight' as the chief source of pleasures and knowledge in rhetoric and poetry; visual detail is the most effective sensory vehicle for the arts and for moving the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ examples from painting, statuary, astronomy and quotations from admired poets (Milton, Virgil) to make loss or gain of sight emotionally vivid. The text argues: 'That is the Sovereign of the Senses... To the Sight we owe not only all the Discoveries of Philosophy, but all the Divine Imagery of Poetry.' Use striking visual passages (e.g., Milton's 'dark, dark, dark') to convey emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for entertaining conversation / 'good company'
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities of agreeable company: patience with dull narrations, occasional bursts of laughter, avoidance of domineering toasts (bumpers) imposed on modest strangers, and freedom from affected vices or feigned defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe occasional, genuine laughter as 'of all other Accomplishments the most requisite'; discourage theatrical display of faults (glorying in insufficiency) and insistent drinking rituals; value neatness ('not ashamed to be clean') and convivial freedom among friends. Use gentle satire (club proposals, exaggerated broken bones) to indicate which behaviours are tiresome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication writing: praise useful public qualities over merely private perfections
rubrics_metrics.description: When dedicating a volume or composing laudatory material, emphasize qualities that make the person 'useful to Society'—public service, diplomatic skill, courage in action—rather than only private accomplishments or bland personal virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate with specific public acts and their social effects (e.g., diplomatic services, military courage, facilitation of commerce), show how these services confer lasting esteem, and keep praise tied to usefulness rather than empty flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a 'familiar' style for epistolary/occasional pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'familiar' mode of writing (the style 'called by the Judicious the Familiar') is appropriate for letters and Spectator-style essays—conversational, personal, and accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct address to the reader, modest first-person anecdotes, short illustrative letters or verses, and an approachable tone. Examples on the page include contributors signing short epistles and verses aimed at social or amorous purposes; the familiar mode invites correspondents and readerly intimacy.
